vignette:
He is a 29-year-old South Asian man who comes to treatment after a mugging that happened on an ordinary evening that still feels, to him, like the moment his life split into before and after. He had been finishing a late painting job, carrying supplies and cash from the day's work, when two men approached him near his car. What starts as a quick request for money becomes threatening in an instant. He remembers the tone of their voices more than their faces, the sharpness in the way one of them closes the distance, the sudden certainty that he is not going to be able to reason his way out of this. He gives them what they ask for, but the fear does not end when they run off. His body keeps bracing as if the attack is still happening, his heart pounding so hard that he can hear it in his ears. He stands there afterward, shaken and humiliated, with the strange, disorienting feeling that the street around him has turned unfamiliar.

In the days that follow, he tries to return to work, telling himself he needs to keep going. Painting has always been the way he supports his family, and before the mugging it is the kind of work that lets him move through a day with rhythm and concentration: preparing walls, taping edges, rolling on even coats of color. Now, he notices every parked car, every cluster of men on the sidewalk, every footstep behind him. He starts taking longer routes to job sites even when they make him late. He double-checks locks, keeps his keys between his fingers when he walks, and scans every space before stepping out of his truck. His wife notices that he is tense at home too, sitting with his back to the wall, jumping when she comes into a room unexpectedly. He tells her he is fine, but he is not. He feels embarrassed by how frightened he has become, as though the mugging took something from him beyond his wallet.

As weeks pass, he begins to feel the event in his body before he can put words to it. A sudden shout from outside makes him flinch. The sound of footsteps closing in behind him can send a wave of panic through his chest. He starts sleeping lightly and waking several times a night, sometimes drenched in sweat, sometimes with no memory of a dream except the feeling that he was being chased. When he does sleep, he wakes tired and already on edge, as if he has not had a break at all. He tries to focus on his work, but his attention slips. He will be painting a wall and realize he has gone over the same section twice, or missed a strip near the ceiling because his mind has drifted back to the moment of being cornered. He becomes more irritable with his wife, not because he wants to be, but because he feels overwhelmed by small demands and then guilty afterward.

He avoids the neighborhood where it happened and refuses to go out after dark unless it is absolutely necessary. He no longer lingers outside after work to talk with neighbors or coworkers. If someone mentions street crime, his chest tightens and he changes the subject. He keeps the details of the mugging mostly to himself, especially the part that haunts him most: how powerless he felt, how quickly he thought about his wife and what would happen if he did not come home. That thought comes back without warning, usually when he is alone. Sometimes he sees the men in flashes-an image crossing his mind while he is showering or standing at the sink-that leaves him stunned and irritable for hours afterward. He feels ashamed of how much the memory controls him, and that shame makes him withdraw even more.

Despite all of this, he keeps showing up. He goes to work because he has to, and he continues to provide for his family, but he does so with a guardedness that now shapes almost every part of his day. He is more watchful than before, slower to trust, and easily startled by ordinary noises. He wants to feel like himself again, the man who could move through the city without calculating every possible threat, but for now he lives with the sense that danger is always just a few steps behind him.
